content.text:
New owners now get customer codes like `ZEL-FRA-0003`: the first three letters of the city, the first three of the last name (both upper-cased), and a 4-digit number counting owners per city. The test suite passes: 3 tests, 0 failures, including the existing acceptance test.

**What changed:**
- **The code itself** (`service/ClinicServiceImpl.java`): when an owner is created, the number is now one more than the count of existing owners in the same city, instead of the count of all owners. City names are compared ignoring case, so "Madison" and "MADISON" share one sequence. Any non-letter characters are skipped when taking the three letters, as the old code already did for last names. For example, "Town12" gives `TOW`.
- **Per-city count**: the code needed a way to count owners in a city, so I added `countByCityIgnoringCase` to `OwnerRepository` and to each of its JPA, JDBC and Spring Data JPA versions.
- **Membership number**: this is still built as `<customerCode>-M<YY>` (YY is the last two digits of the registration year) every time an owner is read, so it picks up the new format with no code change, e.g. `SYD-SMI-0007-M26`. That's the only value I found that's built from the customer code. I updated its comment in `OwnerMapper` and the descriptions and examples in `openapi.yml`.
- **New tests** in `AcceptanceTest`:
  - Two owners are added to one city, then a third (with the city name in different case) gets exactly `ZEL-FRA-0003`; an owner in a new city gets `0001`.
  - The membership number is the new customer code plus `-M<YY>`.

**Things to know:**
- **Existing codes aren't regenerated.** Codes are only assigned when an owner is created, so owners saved under the old format keep their old codes. The seed data has none, so this only affects databases that already have owners created through the API.
- **Duplicates are possible.** If two owners are created in the same city at the same moment, they could get the same number. The old global counter had the same weakness.
- **Short names make shorter codes.** A city or last name with fewer than three letters gives fewer than three characters in that part.

The tests ran only against the default setup (in-memory HSQLDB with JPA), not the JDBC or Spring Data JPA versions.

New owners now get customer codes like `ZEL-FRA-0003`: the first three letters of the city, the first three of the last name (both upper-cased), and a 4-digit number counting owners per city. The test suite passes: 3 tests, 0 failures, including the existing acceptance test.

**What changed:**
- **The code itself** (`service/ClinicServiceImpl.java`): when an owner is created, the number is now one more than the count of existing owners in the same city, instead of the count of all owners. City names are compared ignoring case, so "Madison" and "MADISON" share one sequence. Any non-letter characters are skipped when taking the three letters, as the old code already did for last names. For example, "Town12" gives `TOW`.
- **Per-city count**: the code needed a way to count owners in a city, so I added `countByCityIgnoringCase` to `OwnerRepository` and to each of its JPA, JDBC and Spring Data JPA versions.
- **Membership number**: this is still built as `<customerCode>-M<YY>` (YY is the last two digits of the registration year) every time an owner is read, so it picks up the new format with no code change, e.g. `SYD-SMI-0007-M26`. That's the only value I found that's built from the customer code. I updated its comment in `OwnerMapper` and the descriptions and examples in `openapi.yml`.
- **New tests** in `AcceptanceTest`:
  - Two owners are added to one city, then a third (with the city name in different case) gets exactly `ZEL-FRA-0003`; an owner in a new city gets `0001`.
  - The membership number is the new customer code plus `-M<YY>`.

**Things to know:**
- **Existing codes aren't regenerated.** Codes are only assigned when an owner is created, so owners saved under the old format keep their old codes. The seed data has none, so this only affects databases that already have owners created through the API.
- **Duplicates are possible.** If two owners are created in the same city at the same moment, they could get the same number. The old global counter had the same weakness.
- **Short names make shorter codes.** A city or last name with fewer than three letters gives fewer than three characters in that part.

The tests ran only against the default setup (in-memory HSQLDB with JPA), not the JDBC or Spring Data JPA versions.
